newsitem.title: HUNGARY: MOTOR RACING-HUNGARIAN GP SURVIVES AGAINST THE ODDS.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-HUNGARIAN GP SURVIVES AGAINST THE ODDS.

text.p: It loses money every year, there is no local hero and most of the crowd are foreigners -- but the Hungarian Grand Prix seems to go from strength to strength.

On Sunday, the race will get underway for the 12th time and local organisers are confident the event will stay on the motor racing calendar well into the next century -- and this year might at least break even.
When the first Hungarian Grand Prix was held in 1986, promoters proclaimed it as "Formula One behind the Iron Curtain".

For Bernie Ecclestone, the powerful marketing director of the International Automobile Federation (FIA), moving the multi-million dollar circus into the then Eastern Bloc was both a great publicity stunt and a way into a new market.

For Hungary's communist government, it offered a chance to gain PR points abroad, give their citizens a brief taste of the glamour of the West and generate valuable hard-currency from the thousands of West Germans and Austrians who swarmed to Budapest each August.

But after the change of system in 1989, Hungary became a capitalist democracy and the event lost its novelty. With neighbouring Austria lobbying hard for inclusion on the Formula One roster, the event appeared in jeopardy until a contract was signed in 1995, guaranteeing its existence until 2001.
Even so, organisers know they face a fight to keep hold of the rights to the event.

"There is huge competition for the rights," says Janos Berenyi, chairman of Hungaroring Sport, the Hungarian organisers. "There is growing interest from south-east Asia and South Africa and we know we have to keep bang up-to-date."
They also know they have to keep on the good side of Ecclestone.

Direct pressure from Ecclestone caused the Hungarian organisers to build a new link road from the M3 motorway to the track for use by racers and officials. The old road could no longer cope with the massive crowds the event attracts.
Attila Gaal, Hungaroring Sport's CEO, recently revealed that Michael Schumacher nearly missed the race last year because he could not get through the busy access road.
In addition, almost 10,000 new seats have been built at the Hungaroring, increasing the capacity of the main stands to over 40,000.

But while the improvements may please FIA, they do not help Hungaroring Sport in their struggle to cover their costs. They have to pay $4.6 million for the rights to the event and receive only $1 million from the main sponsors, Marlboro.
With all sponsorship, advertising and television receipts handled centrally by FIA, the Hungarians have to rely on ticket sales and their most loyal supporter -- the Hungarian government.
This year the state has put up 650 million forints ($3.25 million), an increase of 200 million forints on last year's event, but Berenyi believes the government is making a wise investment.
"The Hungarian Grand Prix attracts over 70,000 foreigners to Hungary. They spend billions of forints -- they fill up the hotels and restaurants and they spend money in shops," he said.

"There are people in the world who don't know where Budapest is, but for three days we are at the centre of the sporting world with 130 television stations broadcasting the race and millions watching."

Last year more than 180,000 people attended the Hungarian Grand Prix over the three days. Organisers expect even bigger crowds this time, with estimated ticket receipts of over 800 million forints ($4 million) and the possibility of breaking even for the first time in the race's history.
"We are lucky that Berger won at Hockenheim with Schumacher finishing second." said Berenyi. "Now there will be even more interest in Germany and Austria."
But while the marks and schillings may pour into Budapest this weekend for what promises to be a thrilling race, there is still one missing ingredient for the local sports fans -- a Hungarian.
"It is a very expensive sport," says Berenyi "You need to be a great driver and you need to spend years training and competing, but you cannot ignore the fact that you need money."

In a bid to produce a local favourite with a difference, Hungaroring Sport are supporting what could be Formula One's only third ever woman driver, Judit Forro, who is training and competing in lower rank races in England.
"We have the contract to hold the Grand Prix until 2001 and we hope that within that time, we will see Judit compete in Formula One," said Berenyi.
But the racing fans are willing to be patient and for most, merely hosting the event is enough.

"Of course it would be better to have a Hungarian competitor in the race," says fan Imre Gyetvari, "But everyone has their favourite racers and favourite teams -- the important thing is that Hungary hosts such a major sports event."
